sentences.text: A common pitch for a heat pump ends the same way: it pays for itself.
One HVAC company, Atlas AC, tells its viewers that the extra cost of converting a gas system "could be offset in savings by year five".
In a Skill Builder video about a British home, the verdict is even quicker: "So, four years you got your money back".
Then the Washington Post ran the numbers for one gas-heated house with a basic heat pump, and got a very different answer, "making the payback period around 48 years".
That is not a rounding error.
So which homes get their money back from a heat pump, how fast, and which ones never do?
Pitches like these describe payback as if it were a property of the machine.
Even an electrification group that promotes heat pumps is more careful, telling readers that "a heat pump will often pay off in about 15 years".
And one British owner who publishes detailed running data, Tom Bray, concluded that "a simple calculation would suggest around 18 to 25 years".
Every one of those numbers could be right for the house it describes.
The question is what happens across millions of houses, so that is where we will look: at national models that run the numbers home by home, and at meters in real homes.
Start with a national laboratory model that simulated about 550,000 representative American homes.

Over the life of the equipment and without any subsidy, compared with replacing the old equipment like for like when it wears out, 59 percent came out ahead if every home picked its single best option.

But no real buyer gets to pick with perfect hindsight, and no single heat pump did that well: the cheapest, minimum-efficiency units came out ahead in 55 percent of homes, and the premium cold-climate units in only 21 percent, because their higher price ate the extra savings.
A second national model of single-family houses was harsher still.

It found a heat pump would pay off for about 16.7 million houses, 21 percent of all single-family homes, at the energy prices it assumed, again counting only the extra cost over replacing the old heater with a similar one when it nears the end of its life.
So both figures are already the good-timing case: the heat pump bought at the moment the old equipment would have had to be replaced anyway.
So is it a majority, or a minority?
A third team, mapping energy bills county by county, found 53 percent of households would see lower bills, 19 percent higher ones, and 28 percent no clear change either way.
Even the most generous lifetime figure here, the 59 percent, is a thin majority, and it assumes every home picks its best option.
If only a slim majority of homes come out ahead over the whole life of the equipment, a payback of a few years cannot be the typical case.
Which raises the more useful question: who is in the winning group?
The national lab model names one of the biggest factors, and it is what you heat with today.

For homes that now heat with electricity, fuel oil or propane and already have air conditioning, the national lab model found that almost all would see lower bills, with median savings of $300 to $650 a year.
For gas-heated homes with air conditioning, it depended on the equipment: anywhere from 38 to 99 percent saved on their bills.
The second model put it more bluntly: switching from natural gas "rarely produces a benefit", especially in cold climates.
On oil, the models disagree.

The national lab model, counting the cost of the equipment, found a basic heat pump came out ahead over its life for most homes heated with fuel oil; the second model found a switch from oil "usually causes the homeowner a private economic loss", in part because nearly 65 percent of oil-heated houses are in cold climates.
Meters in New England homes found ductless heat pumps "always operate less expensively than propane heating systems", and cheaper to run than oil too, except on very cold days.
Both of those national figures are already the good-timing case; the field data show what it costs to switch before the old equipment is due.
A Minnesota study priced a cold-climate heat pump with a propane furnace as backup at $9,450 installed, using a national cost database.

Installed while the old furnace and air conditioner still worked, its simple payback came to 14.5 years against an older furnace and 28.8 years against an efficient condensing one, longer than the 18 years the study expects the equipment to last.
Installed when both had failed and needed replacing anyway, the extra cost fell to just $370, and the payback to between 0.6 and 1.1 years.
Same house, same machine, same bills.
The only thing that changed was what you would have had to buy anyway.

The project's later report, from the same Minnesota research, put it plainly: for retrofits, paybacks will typically run "longer than 10 years, unless equipment replacement is necessary", and drop to 5 to 6 years when either the heating or the cooling system has failed.
A model of gas-heated homes in Chicago, Providence, Houston and Oakland, at the energy prices it used, found the same pattern.
Switching paid off for gas customers who "would otherwise need to replace both a furnace and air conditioner simultaneously".

Otherwise, existing gas homes that switched both heating and water heating to electric either paid more for energy, in colder Chicago and Providence, or saved too little to make up the extra cost, in Houston and Oakland.
Put the pieces together and a pattern appears.
If you are leaving propane or electric resistance heat, a heat pump usually pays.

Buying when the old equipment is due for replacement is the case the national figures already describe; in the Minnesota example, with a propane furnace as backup, replacing a failed furnace and air conditioner together cut the payback from decades to about a year.
And if you are tearing out a working gas furnace, the models mostly say it will not pay back on energy savings alone.
There are things that move these numbers.
The first is insulation: for older or leaky homes, Consumer Reports says "it’s always a good idea to first upgrade your insulation and seal any air leaks".
In one group of homes the national lab model examined, sealing and insulating let the medium- and high-efficiency heat pumps be smaller, cutting their installed cost by $2,500 to $4,000.
But the insulation work itself added about $9,000 in that group, so the total upfront cost went up.

It did cut the share of homes whose bills went up with the cheapest units, from 39 percent to 19 percent, and it nudged the lifetime numbers up slightly in cold climates while lowering them in warmer ones.
The second is your own house: the model found the spread between homes in the same place was bigger than the spread between places.
And the savings the model finds depend on local climate and energy prices, so an average is not a forecast for your house.
So what should you do with this?
If you heat with propane or electric baseboards, you are in the group where the models here found the biggest savings, so getting quotes is worth your time.
If your furnace or air conditioner is near the end of its life, that is the moment the extra cost of a heat pump shrinks the most.

And if both are working fine and you heat with gas, switching early is a worse case than anything these models priced; even at replacement time, the second model found gas homes rarely came out ahead, while the national lab model found most gas homes with central air in warmer climates did.
In the model of Chicago, Providence, Houston and Oakland, switching paid off for gas homes that needed a new furnace and air conditioner at the same time, or that paired it with rooftop solar.
Whatever a seller promises, ask one question: payback compared with what, a new furnace and air conditioner, or nothing at all?
So, does a heat pump pay for itself?

For some homes, quickly; for many, never: even when bought at replacement time, one national model found a lifetime gain for 21 percent of all single-family houses, the other for at most 55 percent of homes with any single heat pump.
Which group you are in depends on the fuel you are leaving, the prices where you live, and whether you buy when your old equipment needs replacing anyway.
A quick payback is possible.
It just is not a promise anyone can make about your house before looking at it.
